doc.title: Byron Stripling interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 25, 1998 [interview 1 of 2]

chapter: Count Basie band and Thad Jones
title: Thad Jones as a natural born leader
summary: He describes Thad Jones as a father figure who inspired and pushed the band and conducted charts he had never seen.

story.theme_name: Playing with Count Basie: joining, leading, leaving
story.community_name: Playing with Count Basie: the band, its feel and its people

blocks.x: prices went up and the band was able to survive. Because see they didn’t cut anybody’s salary, they just kept it, so you’ve got to keep a consistent thing coming in, and Thad did very well for the band. And for me it was like I was in heaven. Thad Jones, I’ll just talk about him quickly, was like a father to me. I’ve followed him around like a little puppy. Because there are certain people I think that are born leaders. It’s like they’re put here, okay, you’re going to be a leader. And he was one of those people. A natural born leader. And I sort of just followed him around. And everything he did he could inspire people on the bandstand. It’s really, when I learn that, whatever band or organization there is, it takes upon the tone of the person that stands in front of it. In other words, Thad could be standing in front of the band and it would sound one way. He could leave and Woody Herman would walk in front of the band and it would sound different. The band takes upon — or the orchestra — Seiji Ozawa, he’s going to sound different than if Eugene Ormandy, Eugene, just his presence is going to give — the people know they have to play differently for each person. So what Thad does is he was a natural born leader but he also could push people. And I know with me and I’ve spoken to many lead trumpet players about this, he could just look at you and go Rhhh, like that, and he would pull something out of you. He was a great conductor that way. And he also could make you do more than you thought you could do, which is what leaders are very good at. I remember he would write out these sets and I’d say, “Thad, you’re going play ‘Three Thirty’ and then you’re going to play another tune that’s called ‘Basie’ it’s Ernie Wilkins’ chart, and ‘Shiny Stockings’ then you’re going to play this new tune you wrote and then you’re going to play ‘Whirley-Bird?” Those are all chop busters. He goes, “That’s right up your alley.” And he’d smile. And I’m a young guy, very impressionable, I’m going geez you know he believes I can do this, maybe I can. And when I’d start to get tired he’d just look at me and go Rhhhh! And I’d get this burst of energy. It was like he was throwing electricity at me or something. So I’d go yeah, yeah I could do it. So that’s the kind of magic that a person like that has, in addition to all the musicianship that he had. And the first night that he came on the band he had no reason to be studying old Sammy Nestico charts that we were playing a lot of. He conducted all of them. He didn’t know those charts. He could conduct stuff he’d never even heard before.
